This new qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough

📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a new kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.
  • The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.
  • Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a new kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.

The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.

Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors.

Quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.

Even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.

In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.

Their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.

A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates.

According to recent reports, according to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.

Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, mentioned:.

"We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.

Industry observers note that "The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test.".

Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.

That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.

A Possible Role as Quantum Memory.

According to recent reports, one longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.

Dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, noted:.

"We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.

Industry observers note that "Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system.".

The Next Step Is Building a Prototype.

The team now plans to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.

The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.

The project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.

#274. Industry News: 7 Years Later, Hollywood’s Most Notorious Fantasy Flop Deserves Another Shot

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1401 w)

Industry News: 7 Years Later, Hollywood’s Most Notorious Fantasy Flop Deserves Another Shot

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I vividly remember learning the phrase “uncanny valley” in 2019.
  • Sources indicate that even though I recently got my first dog, I’ve always been a massive cat guy.
  • So for Polygon’s annual Turkey Day celebration, during which we celebrate the “turkeys” that flopped hard but we can’t help but love, I felt obligated to finally watch Cats and write about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I vividly remember learning the phrase “uncanny valley” in 2019. First came the trailer for Sonic the Hedgehog that April, with those alarmingly human teeth. Then came the first trailer for Tom Hooper’s Cats in July. Suddenly, there was a name for a feeling I’d had my whole life. The uncanny valley is that uneasy feeling you get when something looks or moves almost like a real person, but some small detail makes the whole thing feel wrong. That feeling is a lot more common these days, now that AI-generated videos are everywhere. But it was Cats that really brought the uncanny valley into the popular lexicon.

Sources indicate that even though I recently got my first dog, I’ve always been a massive cat guy. I’ve had two cats for almost 16 years. I also love musicals and regularly listen to tracks from Hamilton, Rent, and Dear Evan Hansen. Heck, I also consider myself a Swiftie. By all accounts, Cats seems like something I should have become obsessed with years ago.

So for Polygon’s annual Turkey Day celebration, during which we celebrate the “turkeys” that flopped hard but we can’t help but love, I felt obligated to finally watch Cats and write about it. Was it worth it? I’m still not sure. I can see why Cats earned a measly 19% from critics and 53% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes. The CGI is often distractingly bad, the tonal whiplash is enough to give you a headache, and I’m pretty sure that the story has always been kind of terrible. Despite that, I found the whole thing feverishly fun and, more often than not, surprisingly sexy. (You know, for something with cat people in it.).

Recent findings suggest that victoria (Francesca Hayward) is a young cat abandoned in a London alley. She’s taken in by a group of felines called the Jellicles on the night of their annual ball, during which Old Deuteronomy (Judi Dench) will choose one of them to ascend to the Heaviside Layer and be reborn. The candidates make their cases by performing songs. If you want to know why there’s a cat named Skimbleshanks and what he does on the railway, boy, does he have a number for you.

According to recent reports, there’s a plot in there, especially once Idris Elba, who is genuinely great as Macavity, starts getting rid of the competition with his teleportation powers. (Also, why do some cats have magic powers?) Most of the movie plays like a series of vignettes in which a new cat shows up and sings about the one thing it really wants you to know about itself. That makes some sense for a stage musical adapted from a book of T.S. Eliot poems about different cats. Onscreen, it means the movie keeps asking you to get invested in a new character just as you’ve adjusted to looking at the last one. But because each has a distinct musical styling and energy, the whole thing feels rather uneven and muddled as it shifts between mania and despair on a dime.

Industry observers note that in Cats, everything rides on how much you enjoy spending a few minutes with each cat. Some are delightful. Some are horrible disasters. Hayward, a Royal Ballet dancer when she’s not covered in fur, is exceptional throughout as the newly introduced cat on a dizzying adventure. Steven McRae as Skimbleshanks is probably the most energetic and entertaining of them all. Rebel Wilson as Jennyanydots and James Corden as Bustopher Jones are both the epitome of cringe and perhaps the best examples of why Cats struggles as a movie.

In a recent development, I spent an embarrassing amount of time watching Cats thinking about clothes. Corden’s Bustopher Jones looks like he’s dressed for dinner in a sort of half-tuxedo. Most of the cats just have fur, including Wilson’s Jennyanydots. There’s a moment when she sort of falls off a chair in a way that really plays up the buffoonery of fat cats. Then she rolls onto her back and exposes herself to the camera — it makes you want to shriek and cover your eyes — but then her tail appears strategically propped up between her legs. Not long after, she’s singing into a tail when her actual tail is clearly still behind her. Later in the same number, other cats peel off her outer layer of fur to reveal an outfit underneath, with yet another layer of fur. (WTF?) There’s also a point where she starts eating cockroaches that, like all of the cats, are people in animal costumes. (WTF!?).

I’ve never looked at either of my cats and thought, You are naked. But the Jellicles have human faces and mostly human bodies. There are no visible nipples or genitals. Why are some fully clothed? Why are some partially clothed? Does the existence of the clothing make the others seem even more naked than before? Why does there appear to be a correlation between a cat’s age and the amount of clothing they wear? Why didn’t the production design commit fully to one extreme or the other?

In a recent development, one of the funniest things I’ve ever heard was a rumor that, at one point, all of these cats had buttholes. According to an anonymous crew member whose account was reported by Vanity Fair in March 2020, the simulated skin and fur folded in ways that accidentally resembled buttholes and genitals in roughly a dozen unfinished shots. An anonymous visual-effects editor told The Daily Beast that one crew member was literally brought in to remove all of the buttholes. #ReleaseTheButtholeCut.

Recent findings suggest that jason Derulo’s Rum Tum Tugger was the first cat I was genuinely excited to spend a whole song with. Derulo plays him like a guy who knows everybody in the room is looking at him and would be insulted if they stopped. There’s even a part where Victoria is dancing with her leg stretched up into the air. He leans his face in. For a fleeting moment, you can’t tell if he’s going to use her foot as a microphone or suck on her toes​​​​​​​. For a certain kind of pervert, Cats can get decidedly sexy. It wants your mind to go there on more than one occasion.

Industry observers note that when Taylor Swift demonstrates up rather late in the movie as Bombalurina and dumps catnip on a room full of cats, the sexual energy is dizzying. The song itself is mediocre at best, but the vibes are immaculate. There’s something refreshing about a number where the movie seems fully aware of how horny it’s being. For a few minutes, I stopped trying to figure out how anybody’s fur worked and just enjoyed the song. (Is this Taylor Swift’s sexiest music video ever? Probably.).

The biggest bit of tonal whiplash comes with Jennifer Hudson’s Grizabella. Hudson has an incredible voice (she’s an EGOT winner!​​​​​​​) and really gives it her all for “Memory,” but Grizabella spends every one of her scenes scream-cry-singing about feelings of rejection and lamenting her lost life as a really cool cat. Hudson once told Empire that she had no idea her character would have ears or a tail, and all of the snot pouring out of her face​​​​​​​ is real. It’s powerful stuff, but also dreadfully unappealing. For me, similar numbers work in something like Les Misérables, where​​​​​​​ the narrative builds up to powerful emotional beats. In Cats, it just feels like a total buzzkill. It made me grateful that Old Deuteronomy selected Grizabella as the Jellicle Choice, which itself feels like a bizarre form of ritual sacrifice and rebirth, if only so she would stop.

Seven years after learning the phrase “uncanny valley,” I finally understand why people wanted to watch Cats together and yell at the screen. My wife refused to watch it with me, so every time I wanted to turn to somebody and say, “Did you see that?” I had to sit there alone with whatever I’d just seen. More often than not, I was pleasantly uncomfortable.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve seen people argue that Cats falls short of “so bad it’s good.” I think it gets there. It helps if you’re willing to embrace the silly fun and admit that people wearing digital fur can be kind of sexy​​​​​​​. Does that make me a furry?

  • The 31-year-old woman, identified as Hana, had gone for a walk through Glückaufpark in Gelsenkirchen on October 25 to clear her head after becoming overwhelmed by financial and academic pressures.
  • The chemistry student eventually broke down in tears, taking a seat on a bench at the playground and calling her aunt.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A woman in Germany was slapped with a €25 ($27 USD) fine after sitting down on a bench at a children’s playground to cry, unaware that she was breaking the law by being there without a child.

The 31-year-old woman, identified as Hana, had gone for a walk through Glückaufpark in Gelsenkirchen on October 25 to clear her head after becoming overwhelmed by financial and academic pressures.

The chemistry student eventually broke down in tears, taking a seat on a bench at the playground and calling her aunt.

“I just wanted to be alone and not be seen by anyone,” she told German broadcaster WDR.

Recent findings suggest that however, three municipal enforcement officers approached her and asked whether two boys playing on the swings were her children. When she said no, the officers demanded her identification and issued her a €25 fine.

Under Gelsenkirchen’s municipal regulations, playgrounds are reserved for children aged 14 and under, along with their parents, guardians, and supervisors.

While there was a sign outlining the playground’s rules, BILD reports that it did not explicitly state that unaccompanied adults were prohibited from sitting on the benches.

Hana argued that the officers could have simply asked her to move instead of issuing a fine.

“I felt as though I was worth nothing as a human being,” she said.

According to recent reports, despite criticism, the city defended the officers’ actions, describing the fine as relatively mild and proportionate. According to WELT, Hana has since paid the fine to avoid incurring additional costs.

Rather than relaxing the rules, the city council discussed increasing the maximum penalty for playground violations from €55 to €60 ($66) on November 17.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023.
  • John Motson commentated on hundreds of football games over the course of five different decades, starting in the 1970s.
  • But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023.

John Motson commentated on hundreds of football games over the course of five different decades, starting in the 1970s. The English commentator then became the mainstay voice of EA's dominant football simulation series, beginning with FIFA 96 all the way up until FIFA 2005, when the publisher decided to go in a different direction.

But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family. An upgrade with Motson's voice will go live on 26th November. "There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," senior game designer director Mat Prior said in a statement given to the BBC earlier today.

Recent findings suggest that "At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back," Prior added, explaining that Motson's posthumous role in the game is being handled with a mixture of previously recorded voice lines and AI. EA supposedly went down the AI route since it doesn't have recordings of Motson commentating over newer, more fresh faced footballers.

Fred Motson said it "means an awful lot" to hear his dad's voice in the game again, and he reckons his dad was "always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects," even if he wasn't the most technologically savvy person. EA said it had paid the family for the rights to use Motson's voice and likeness.

In a recent development, save Our Voices Now founder Peter Caulfield - who campaigns for the government to regulate the use of generative AI voice cloning tech - told the BBC he wasn't comfortable with the project. "In life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed," he stated. "Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either." He doesn't have a problem with actors consenting to AI voice replication while they're still alive, however.

A Japanese acting union recently fought back against this very same practice by proposing fresh guidelines that would stop the replication of dead actors' voices without their permission.

Sources indicate that generative AI has been widely controversial in the games industry for other reasons, too. In recent months, there's been a huge impact on smaller game developers who are worried that their games could be cloned by AI copycats and some who have had to delay their release dates because of Steam's growing approvals backlog.

"The Grounds comes across as a frippery, Ultimate Team rumbles ever on, but FC 27 brings meaningful changes to the fluidity and speed of play. Given that its practical football-game monopoly is more or less unchallenged, EA could do a lot less than this," Josh Wise wrote in Eurogamer's EA Sports FC 27 review.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use.
  • Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

The thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.

It could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

According to recent reports, this is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

Sources indicate that if you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be.

The reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this upcoming platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac.

Industry observers note that december's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

According to the late, great astronomer Fred Espenak, the Cold Moon will be just 221,667 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth when it turns full, making it the closest supermoon of 2026!

The full Cold Supermoon will make for a spectacular sight when it rises over the eastern horizon at sunset on Dec. 23, mere hours before reaching maximum illumination. Remember to use Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

In a recent development, earth's satellite may appear larger than normal while close to the horizon. This is partly because it is near perigee, when it appears subtly larger in the night sky, but also because of a phenomenon called the moon illusion, which tricks us into perceiving the moon to be bigger than it actually is while in the presence of foreground objects.

According to recent reports, the moon may also adopt a striking golden or orange hue around moonrise and moonset. When the moon is low on the horizon, its light travels through more of Earth's atmopshere, scattering shorter, bluer wavelengths of light and allowing longer, redder wavelengths to reach our eyes.

The table below details moonrise timings for a selection of cities spread across the globe for Dec. 23-24:.

The December full moon is often called the Cold Moon in reference to the often freezing temperatures that can descend this time of the year. It's also known as the "Long Night Moon" by the Mohican tribe of North America, because of its proximity to the winter solstice, which marks the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere.

Old English peoples knew it as the "Moon Before Yule", according to Time and Date, while the Celts of Europe referred to it as the Oak Moon after traditions that centered around the hardy trees.

The December full moon also coincides with the Hindu festival of Datta Jayanti, when followers gather to celebrate the birth of Lord Dattatreya, who embodies the Hindu holy trinity of Lord Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, according to the Government of Maharashtra. The December full moon also rises close to the Christian celebration of Christmas on Dec. 25, when followers celebrate the birth of Jesus Christ.

Recent findings suggest that the Cold Moon will shine in the center of a majestic "Winter Hexagon" of stars bright enough to easily cut through the glare cast by the lunar disk after it rises on Nov. 24.

It has been revealed that begin by locating Sirius, the brightest star in our night sky, which rises into the southeastern sky shortly after 8 p.m. local time for viewers in New York. Next, trace an imaginary line to the blue supergiant star Rigel in the nearby constellation Orion, before hopping to the orange glow of Aldebaran, which represents an eye of the great bull depicted in the constellation Taurus.

Next we move to Capella, the jewel of the constellation Auriga, before jumping down to Pollux in the constellation Gemini and nearby Procyon, before closing the loop with Sirius once more.

Jupiter and the red light of Mars will shine low in the eastern sky in the hour before midnight, while Saturn will lurk close to the western horizon. Look to the southeast just before dawn to spot Venus appearing as a brilliant "Morning Star", with the red giant Arcturus shining higher in the predawn sky close to the constellation Bootes.

The December full moon presents a stunning opportunity to photograph the lunar disk as it shines in Earth's sky entirely free from shadow. #268. Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold

Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it.
  • The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.

The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.

Recent findings suggest that the Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.

A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959.

In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.

In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.

Sources indicate that quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.

The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.

Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.

Sources indicate that these theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly vital in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.

In a recent development, the challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.

It has been revealed that quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.

How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment.

Recent findings suggest that the Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.

Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.

The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.

Recent findings suggest that the second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.

Industry observers note that by combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.

Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an key interaction between matter and magnetic flux.

Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.

Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.

It has been revealed that initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.

Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.

"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," claims Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics.".

What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.

A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion.

With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.

Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.

When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.

Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.

The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.

This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.

The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment demonstrated how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.

A Fresh Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics.

The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.

The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.

Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.

Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.

By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.

The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.

Also: Google is making it easier to opt out of Gemini AI training.

Recent findings suggest that newly introduced to Google’s AI Mode is an option known as temporary threads. By choosing this setting, any searches you conduct in AI mode are detached from your own Google account and history. Your temporary searches won’t be affected by your past preferences or chats. They won’t be impacted by any personalization you’ve set up through your account. And they won’t be saved to your chat history. The goal here is to prevent anyone else, including Google, from accessing your conversations in this mode.

This option is presently rolling out around the world in all languages to Google search on both desktop and mobile browsers. You can run a temporary thread on any device and in any browser.

Industry observers note that try this for yourself: Head to the regular Google search page and click the button on the search field for AI Mode. You should then see an icon with a pen hovering over a dotted circle. If you don’t see it, you may have to run a search to get started. On the results page, you should then spot the icon.

Recent findings suggest that hover over the icon, and the tooltip will say: “Start temporary thread.” Click the icon on the left to start a newly introduced thread. Now, any conversation you kick off will be temporary and unconnected to your account. But you don’t have to stick with just plain old text. Select the plus icon to upload an image or file. Select the microphone icon to speak instead of type.

Sources indicate that are these temporary threads truly private? Here’s what Google says:.

Industry observers note that “Temporary threads will not be saved to your Google account and disappear after 24 hours,” Google said on a support page. “They won’t be used to train Google’s generative AI models, unless you submit feedback or it’s necessary for safety purposes. Google will still collect data and use data that is not associated with your account, including to keep our services working smoothly and safely and to support business operations.”.

Google also warns that your browser may still save your history if you visit a website within a temporary thread. Data could still be collected by the sites you visit and the services those sites use, including Google services like Google Analytics.

For those reasons, you should still be cautious about the information you share even in a temporary thread. But certainly, this option provides greater privacy and protection than a regular AI Mode search.

  • Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their substantial RPGs and set a fresh "gold standard.".

In a recent development, the upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon. Playground Games had to set up an entirely upcoming team to work on its fairytale revival, so Fable's production wasn't quite as smooth sailing as the studio's consistently excellent Forza Horizon series, for example.

Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.

Recent findings suggest that "In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard," Fulton said. "And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG.".

"All of these games continue to reset player expectations," he continued. Millions of players suddenly had certain expectations about what their major-budget, open-world role-playing games should look like. So, Playground couldn't pull inspiration from Fable and Fable alone.

"I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects," Fulton added.

Still, Playground's Fable is drawing most heavily from Lionhead's Fable. Fulton specifically mentions the game's signature British wit and in-flux morality system as examples. Then there's also the spontaneous life sim elements that "none of our competitors do," according to Fulton. "It's a totally Fable thing, the social simulation and economic simulation. Okay, there are games that have economic simulations, but they're not in [our] RPG category. Fable is unique in that it's almost like a life sim in terms of genre.".

Raising four separate families and becoming the entire map's benevolent landlord was one of the funnest parts of Fable back in the day, alongside those sometimes silly characters. Seeing next year's Fable lean into those systemic choices, and having Albion's NPCs react to them more believably, could give this one a very long shelf life.

#262. 32 Years Later, Disney's Most Notorious Cash-Grab Sequel Is Better Than You Remember

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1129 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

32 Years Later, Disney's Most Notorious Cash-Grab Sequel Is Better Than You Remember

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1129 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Polygon)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ever since former Disney CEO Bob Chapek released his autobiography last September, a rather unexpected Disney movie has been a topic for discussion: the direct-to-VHS sequel to Aladdin titled The Return of Jafar.
  • While these sequels — especially The Return of Jafar — were highly profitable for Disney, some felt that they cheapened the work of Disney’s theatrical division.
  • In a recent development, since then, most Disney fans have come to agree that stopping these movies was for the best, but Chapek, who was in charge of that division for Disney, is still bitter about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ever since former Disney CEO Bob Chapek released his autobiography last September, a rather unexpected Disney movie has been a topic for discussion: the direct-to-VHS sequel to Aladdin titled The Return of Jafar. Released in 1994, The Return of Jafar was the first in a long line of direct-to-VHS (and later direct-to-DVD) sequels to theatrical Disney films. Besides Aladdin, Disney made sequels to The Lion King, The Little Mermaid, Pocahontas, Mulan, and several other then-modern Disney animated features, as well as some much older classics like Cinderella and Bambi. These movies used cheaper animation produced by Disney’s TV division​​​​​​​ and were developed in far less time than Disney spends developing animated feature films​​​​​​​.

While these sequels — especially The Return of Jafar — were highly profitable for Disney, some felt that they cheapened the work of Disney’s theatrical division. Their chief critic was Pixar head John Lasseter, and when Disney acquired Pixar in 2006, Lasseter convinced CEO Bob Iger to shut down the operation.

In a recent development, since then, most Disney fans have come to agree that stopping these movies was for the best, but Chapek, who was in charge of that division for Disney, is still bitter about it. In a chapter Chapek titled “Jafar Returns, and I Emerge,” he writes: “Why was there such vocal criticism aimed at the movie? Likely because a bunch of upstart TV animators in their twenties had created something that generated five times the profits of a typical theatrical release … It was Bob from Flyover Indiana, educated at a state school, who disrupted the business and kept the studio afloat with an endeavor others had dismissed as creative heresy.”.

Industry observers note that while Chapek’s bitterness is palpable, he’s right about the profitability of The Return of Jafar​​​​​​​, which cost just $5 million to produce and raked in more than $300 million. And while I personally agree that these poorly made sequels​​​​​​​ cheapened the integrity of the originals, I do have a soft spot specifically for The Return of Jafar — but not because it made so much money.

I was seven years old when Aladdin came out and it quickly became my favorite Disney movie (and it still is). I loved everything about it and even collected the Aladdin action figures by Mattel (including the Genie, which included a cool feature where you could pull out his head and swap his expression with another head stored inside his body). The Return of Jafar came out about 18 months after Aladdin, and I loved the story about Jafar as a genie seeking revenge on Aladdin and the other characters. Sure, Genie seemed a bit different in the sequel (he was played by Homer Simpson voice actor Dan Castellaneta instead of Robin Williams), but he was still my favorite character and still very funny.

Back then, I was too young and dumb to notice the difference between Aladdin and The Return of Jafar from a quality standpoint, but over time — after parting with my Aladdin action figures and gaining a greater appreciation for the process behind Disney's animated films — I grew to understand why Return of Jafar isn’t so good.

However, I’ve since come to fall in love with it all over again for another reason: Gilbert Gottfried.

While Williams didn’t return for The Return of Jafar, the rest of the Aladdin cast did, including comedian Gilbert Gottfried as Iago​​​​​​​, the scheming parrot who sat on Jafar’s shoulders in the first film.

Iago was no longer Jafar’s sidekick in the sequel. Instead, he abandons Jafar in the beginning of the movie, as he’s fed up with getting bossed around and hates living inside of a lamp (where Jafar is imprisoned). Iago pulls himself out of the lamp and comes up with a scheme to ingratiate himself with Aladdin, Jasmine, and the others so he can live a cushy life in the palace. And while his proposal is entirely cynical at first, he does find himself caring for the humans he opposed in the first film, especially Aladdin, who seems​​​​​​​ most willing to give him a second chance.

Industry observers note that eventually, Jafar finds a fresh stooge in the bumbling thief Abis Mal, who finds Jafar’s lamp and begins making hasty wishes. His first wish is for the sunken treasure ship Coeur du Mer, and Jafar teleports him deep into the ocean. Abis Mal then has to use his second wish so he doesn’t drown. As Jafar tells Abis Mal to take some time on his third wish, Jafar plots his takeover of Agrabah and even, temporarily, lures Iago back into his ranks.

As surprising as it might sound, The Return of Jafar is an Iago story first and foremost. He has a more developed character arc than anyone else in the entire movie, and the writers managed to evolve the character without undermining his established self-interest or making him any less funny. He also has two songs that Gottfried scream-sings, and they’re both still hilarious and more catchy than you might think. (“I’m Lookin’ Out for Me”​​​​​​​ is especially great.).

My renewed affection for The Return of Jafar came about in the late 2010s​​​​​​​ when I began listening to Gilbert Gottfried's Amazing Colossal Podcast, where Gottfried and his co-host Frank Santopadre interviewed showbiz legends every week. Up until that podcast, I had only a vague awareness of Gottfried’s career, mostly as a voice actor, but within a few years he became one of my all-time favorite comedians. As a result, I sought out​​​​​​​ many of his best film and TV roles and, while there were many, Gottfried almost never starred in something. His major personality and raging voice were mostly reserved for small, hilarious cameos. He was never the leading man — except in The Return of Jafar.

(I also encourage everyone to watch the 2017 documentary Gilbert, which is a touching portrait of the man.).

Recent findings suggest that and since Gottfried died in 2022 of Myotonic Dystrophy Type 2, my defense of The Return of Jafar has turned downright personal. Yes, on an objective level, I can recognize the rushed narrative and inferior animation. More broadly, I understand and agree with the idea that Disney’s direct-to-video era hurt Disney’s​​​​​​​ overall artistic legacy, and that The Return of Jafar was the start of all that. But over the past few months, as Disney fans come out against Chapek’s profit-first, art-second defense by bashing this movie all over again, I can't help but think of Iago’s best song lyric from The Return of Jafar, where the aggressive parrot​​​​​​​ shouts, “I'm through with that! I'm flappin' free! From here on in, I'm lookin' out for me!”.

The Return of Jafar is streaming on Disney Plus.

Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa.
  • Industry observers note that the findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.

Industry observers note that the findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.

Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters.

One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.

Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.

In a recent development, scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.

The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.

In a recent development, "Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," remarked Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.

"You just have to prepare it in the right way.

It has been revealed that "Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.

"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.

"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality.".

Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin.

Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.

Recent findings suggest that physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.

The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.

In a recent development, under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.

Industry observers note that "It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself.".

Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.

The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light.

To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.

Sources indicate that dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.

According to recent reports, "To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he stated. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature.".

The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.

Industry observers note that this underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.

As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.

The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.

In a recent development, "This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.

Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications.

The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.

One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically key molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.

The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.

Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.

According to recent reports, other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.

It has been revealed that "The implications are wide-ranging," remarked Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.

"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.

"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.

"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.

These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.

A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed.

For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.

By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.

The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.

According to recent reports, "For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," mentioned Dr. Forbes.

"And astonishingly, this fresh behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen.".

The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.

The ultimate monitor for CS2 and Valorant: What actually matters?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in competitive shooters like Counter-Strike 2, Valorant, and Call of Duty, every millisecond counts.
  • It has been revealed that but while graphics cards usually get most of the attention, your monitor plays a huge role in how smooth and responsive a game feels.
  • Industry observers note that with gaming monitors now hitting 480Hz and beyond, refresh rates are reaching some pretty astonishing numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in competitive shooters like Counter-Strike 2, Valorant, and Call of Duty, every millisecond counts. Players are constantly looking for ways to get an edge, whether that’s upgrading their PC, tweaking settings, or investing in a faster monitor.

It has been revealed that but while graphics cards usually get most of the attention, your monitor plays a huge role in how smooth and responsive a game feels. After all, there’s only so much benefit to pushing hundreds of frames per second if your display can’t keep up.

Industry observers note that with gaming monitors now hitting 480Hz and beyond, refresh rates are reaching some pretty astonishing numbers. But you might be asking, can you actually feel the difference, and is upgrading from 144Hz or 240Hz really worth it?

In competitive shooters, where quick reactions and precise aiming matter, a monitor’s refresh rate can influence how smoothly movement appears on screen.

Sources indicate that A higher refresh rate allows the display to enhancement its image more frequently. For example, a 144Hz monitor refreshes approximately every 6.94 milliseconds, while a 480Hz display refreshes every 2.08 milliseconds.

That difference can help players track moving opponents and receive updated visual information sooner, particularly in fast-paced games like Counter-Strike 2 and Valorant.

However, the benefits become smaller at higher refresh rates, and players need a PC capable of producing enough frames to take full advantage of them.

Refresh rate isn’t the only factor affecting motion clarity, either. OLED panels generally offer much faster pixel response times than traditional LCD monitors, reducing the ghosting that can appear behind moving objects.

Why you should upgrade to an OLED for GTA 6.

The best gaming monitor in 2024: Budget, 4K & Ultrawide.

The best refresh rate for Counter-Strike 2.

GIGABYTE’s AORUS ELITE lineup combines those fast response times with high refresh rates, offering different options depending on how players use their monitors.

The AORUS FO32U24G features a 32-inch fourth-generation Tandem WOLED panel with a 0.03ms GTG response time. Its Dual Mode technology allows players to switch between two display configurations:.

Industry observers note that this approach could appeal to players who regularly switch between different genres. Someone playing Counter-Strike 2 might prefer the 480Hz mode, while a player enjoying a visually demanding single-player game could switch back to 4K.

The smaller AORUS FO27Q28G takes a different approach, offering a 27-inch QHD Tandem WOLED panel with a 280Hz refresh rate and the same advertised 0.03ms GTG response time.

Both monitors also support NVIDIA G-SYNC compatibility and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, which can help reduce tearing when frame rates fluctuate.

Refresh rate and response time aren’t the only specifications to focus on.

Modern gaming monitors increasingly include built-in features designed to give players more control over visibility, screen layout, and the information displayed during gameplay.

GIGABYTE’s AORUS ELITE monitors include several Tactical Features intended for different competitive scenarios:.

Some of these features may be particularly relevant to Counter-Strike 2 players, many of whom have specific preferences for screen size, resolution, and aspect ratio.

Tactical Switch 2.0 allows players to change between different display configurations without manually adjusting every setting, while Tactical HUD could be useful in games where players regularly need to reference mini-maps or other on-screen information.

GIGABYTE also includes Night Vision and AI Black Equalizer to improve visibility in darker environments, alongside Ultra Clear, which uses black-frame insertion to reduce perceived motion blur.

Not every feature will be useful to every player, and some display-side assists may be restricted under competitive tournament rules. Players should check the rules of the games and competitions they participate in before using them.

Although 480Hz monitors offer extremely frequent display updates, not every competitive player needs the highest available refresh rate.

For someone upgrading from a 60Hz or 75Hz display, even moving to 144Hz can make a substantial difference in perceived smoothness.

Players already using 240Hz or 280Hz monitors may notice a smaller improvement when switching to 480Hz, particularly if their PC struggles to maintain the frame rates required to take advantage of it.

A 480Hz monitor makes the most sense for players who prioritize competitive performance and have a PC capable of producing extremely high frame rates. For others, a 280Hz OLED may provide a better balance between responsiveness, resolution, and everyday use.

GIGABYTE’s M series offers several alternatives depending on panel technology, screen finish, and gaming preferences:.

The MO27Q2A provides a QD-OLED alternative for players who want fast response times and high refresh rates, while the MO27Q28G and MO27Q28GR offer different screen finishes depending on the environment.

The M27UP takes a different approach with an IPS panel, making it an option for players who want 4K gaming and high-refresh competitive performance without moving to OLED.

For players considering OLED, long-term panel care is another factor worth keeping in mind.

Sources indicate that competitive shooters frequently display static interface elements, including health bars, ammunition counters, mini-maps, and scoreboards. Over extended periods, these elements can contribute to uneven pixel wear.

GIGABYTE’s AORUS ELITE FO32U24G and FO27Q28G feature AI OLED Care Pro, which includes automated pixel cleaning, brightness adjustments, and display protection designed to reduce burn-in risk.

The MO27Q2A, MO27Q28G, and MO27Q28GR instead feature AI OLED Care, providing background panel maintenance and protection.

While 480Hz OLED monitors represent a high-performance option for competitive gaming, they aren’t necessarily the right choice for everyone.

Players who spend most of their time in Counter-Strike 2 or Valorant and have PCs capable of producing hundreds of frames per second may benefit from the additional responsiveness.

For those who split their time between competitive shooters and visually demanding single-player games, a lower-refresh OLED with higher resolution may make more sense.

Ultimately, the best gaming monitor isn’t always the one with the highest refresh rate. It’s the one that matches the games you play, the hardware you own, and the experience you’re trying to achieve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that linux is all about choice. From the kernel all the way up to the desktop environment, you get to determine what is used and even how it is used. The staggering number of distributions, desktops, package managers, file managers, and terminal apps provide you with a nearly infinite combination of choices. That choice is and has always been a key aspect of Linux.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me.

So too is innovation. If there’s one thing that separates Linux from all other operating systems, it’s the willingness to try something different. Linux developers are always pushing the limits of what an operating system is, and this fresh take on the OS is the epitome of that.

Sources indicate that the distribution in question is called Pond. According to the developers, “Pond is an opportunity for us to play with familiar conventions and experiment with latest ideas that make a computer more natural and satisfying.”.

The developers have achieved something special. Pond takes the standard UI and turns it on its head. Part tiling window manager, part mobile UI, part GNOME, and part something we’ve never before seen, this desktop environment is special. It took me all of five minutes to fall in love with what they’ve created.

The Pond UI consists of the following:.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend.

If you’ve ever considered using a tiling window manager, but thought the lack of a mouse made it seem a bit too complicated, Pond is exactly what you want. Here’s how it works:.

In a recent development, pond uses the Niri window manager to arrange windows in columns along an infinite strip from left to right. In multi-monitor setups, each display gets its own strip, so windows never “overflow” from one monitor to the next.

Also: How to install Arch Linux without losing your mind.

Sources indicate that at the same time, workspaces are dynamic, and there’s always a newly introduced workspace automatically created to the right of the farthest-right window. The combination of the Pond sidebar and Niri’s way of handling windows makes this UI truly original.

Pond doesn’t have a traditional desktop menu. Instead, you open the launcher (using the Super+Space key combination), type the name of the app you want to install, and hit Enter when the app name appears on both the display and as an icon in the top portion of the sidebar.

Recent findings suggest that another thing that sets Pond apart is how you install apps. Yes, you can open a terminal window and install an app using the pacman command, or you can open the launcher, type install, press Enter, and then type the name of the app you want to install. For instance, if you wanted to install LibreOffice, you would type:.

Sources indicate that once you hit Enter a second time, the installation will begin. Many apps install via Flatpak, but on the off-chance an app must be installed via the pacman package manager, you’ll be prompted to type your user password before the installation begins.

As I hinted earlier, Pond is based on Arch Linux, which means it’s a rolling-release distribution. One glitch that did give me pause was the lack of a GUI update system, which indicates that updates would have to happen in the terminal, like so:.

I installed the Shelly GUI frontend, which does have an update component. Personally, I would simply open the terminal window, type sudo pacman -Syu, hit Enter, and let the update run in the background. But if a GUI is your jam, Shelly is what you want.

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux.

Industry observers note that it would be sweet if the developers allowed updating the system from within the launcher, so it didn’t require opening the terminal first. The Pond launcher does allow running system commands from the launcher, which will then open the terminal window and execute the command. For instance, open the terminal, type a command, hit Enter, and then scroll through the list of available commands that can be run.

Pond ships with kernel 7.3.4-3, so it has outstanding hardware recognition and performance.

You should definitely give Pond a try, especially if you’re adventurous and want to experience something completely different. If, on the other hand, different is not in your stream, then Pond will frustrate you to no end.

Also: Why Nextcloud Office is my newly introduced favorite free productivity suite.

Pond excited me more than any OS has in a very long time; so much so that I could see this becoming my go-to OS, once it reaches stable release. Until then, I will keep Pond installed on a laptop, keep upgrading, and see what happens next.

Kudos to the Pond OS team for coming up with something truly unique in an already competitive world.

Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6.

Recent findings suggest that in the week ending 14th November, PS5 hardware unit sales registered a 2.4x increase over the same week last year. That's according to industry analyst Mat Piscatella at Circana, who pulled the data from Circana's retail tracking service, which covers the US retail market.

The PS5 Pro only accounted for less than 10 percent of the PlayStation's total unit sales, by the way, which Piscatella noted was "a LOT better than it has been in recent weeks", and seemingly the result of increased supply.

According to recent reports, GTA 6, of course, released on 19th November, so the surge in console hardware sales was clearly driven by the rush to attain consoles before the game came out. And while the GTA 6-driven demand isn't surprising, it's worth noting how much more expensive PS5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles are today.

Industry observers note that A standard PS5 today costs $650, compared to $550 a year ago. The PS5 Pro saw a substantial jump from $750 last November to $900 today. The base Xbox Series X jumped from $650 last year to $800 today, while Series S now costs $500, up from $400.

Even Switch 2, where GTA 6 is not available, saw a notable boost of 40 percent in hardware sales over the same period, driven by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and the special edition Zelda Switch 2 console.

According to recent reports, circana's November US video game market report, which releases in December, is already one of the most anticipated this year, for digesting and documenting the GTA 6 effect. Worldwide, GTA 6 sold more than 32.5m copies in one day, making Rockstar's parent manufacturer Take-Two $3.79bn (£2.89bn) in revenue. We haven't had any updated official sales figures since; but estimates suggest the sales figure could be well into the 40-millions. Perhaps Rockstar is waiting to hit the nice round 50m sales mark before announcing it.
