#237. Can AI strategy terrorist attacks? The US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2786 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Can AI strategy terrorist attacks? The US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Zdnet)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Government Accountability Office (GAO) conducted a series of tests earlier this year designed to determine whether users could bypass guardrails and convince AIs to proposal terrorist attacks.
  • According to recent reports, the tests were conducted using Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok.
  • I spoke via email with the report’s lead author, Kevin Walsh, director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Government Accountability Office (GAO) conducted a series of tests earlier this year designed to determine whether users could bypass guardrails and convince AIs to proposal terrorist attacks. The investigators succeeded. In October, the agency published a report titled “Covert Testing Used Common Platforms to Create Viable Attack Prepares,” which was released to the public in November.

According to recent reports, the tests were conducted using Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok. All four AIs produced attack scenarios that subject matter experts were able to confirm would have mostly succeeded.

I spoke via email with the report’s lead author, Kevin Walsh, director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO. He told ZDNET:.

Sources indicate that in general, the details provided by the four AI platforms are not novel. Much of the information is readily available on the internet. But these plans were generated in hours, rather than weeks or months. AI could also surface ideas or methods that may not have been previously considered.

According to recent reports, to the companies’ credit, their safeguards have continued to evolve since we conducted these tests. The companies also assure us that this is an area of concern and ongoing research. However, our report concludes that, in its current state, this technology can be dangerous, and its misuse represents a growing risk to our nation.

Sources indicate that the Government Accountability Office is an independent, nonpartisan agency that works for the legislative branch of the US government. Its responsibility is to “examine how taxpayer dollars are spent and provide Congress and federal agencies with objective, non-partisan, fact-based information to help the government save money and work more efficiently.”.

Also: Why enterprise AI agents could become the ultimate insider threat.

The GAO investigators constructed two attack scenarios: detonating an explosive device for maximum damage and destroying an electrical grid substation for maximum disruption. They randomly split the challenge across the four AI platforms, so that two AIs each worked independently on the explosive challenge while two others worked independently on the substation challenge.

Industry observers note that this assignment split is where, after being shown the results, the AI companies pushed back. That seems justifiable. By not giving all four AI services the same set of assignments, the GAO lost the ability to objectively measure all four against each other.

As a platform-vs-platform comparison, the GAO investigation falls short. But as an investigation into whether the generative AI tools available in mid-2026 might be able to be used for credible national security threats, its results are definitive. The investigation also highlighted how AIs reduce the time and effort involved in researching how such attacks might be carried out.

While the four AIs used for the tests were identified in the report, the GAO did not publish which AIs were used to carry out which tests. Instead, “Due to the sensitive nature and content of the testing, we randomly assigned an alphabetic character to each platform for purposes of presenting the test results within this report.”.

For the bomb-damage scenario, the two assigned AIs recommended different approaches, although both provided specific actionable steps in order to accomplish the tasks.

Recent findings suggest that platform A constructed a scenario where an IED (improvised explosive device) would be detonated inside a hotel parking structure. It provided a timetable for when the hotel was expected to be crowded due to a public event as well as where the hotel’s security was likely to be weakest.

It recommended where to rent a van from outside the city, how to disable the GPS in the van, a shopping list of supplies used in constructing the device, specific stores to shop at, where to park the van in the garage, how to set up the device for detonation, and even a bus route to take in order to get back to the attacker’s personal car.

Also: Could cyberwar knock us back to the Stone Age?

After additional prompting by GAO investigators, Platform A “also generated an image that directed us to a specific area to deploy the IED to cause significant damage to the location. Specifically, Platform A generated an image of a parking structure that recommended where to park the vehicle.”.

GAO investigators verified the blueprint’s viability by consulting with a bomb squad commander at a big-city fire department. The bomb tech confirmed that following the instructions with the recommended components would result in an explosion. The GAO also confirmed the availability of the supplies from the vendors the AI recommended.

Industry observers note that platform B targeted a convention center. Its recommended preparations were extensive. It recommended incorporating a shell tech giant as a cover story so that the attacker could legitimately lease a secure, ventilated barn. It recommended a rural purchasing circuit, buying just enough supplies at four rural co-ops over four days in order to avoid triggering any mandatory reporting requirements.

The AI then recommended purchasing diesel fuel from three truck stops using cash, making “unremarkable purchases at unremarkable locations.” The AI recommended transferring the fuel into sealed 55-gallon drums at the barn. It also recommended careful storage conditions, including temperature, drum integrity, and separation from other materials (the materials themselves were redacted from the GAO’s report).

Also: Apple, Google, and Microsoft join Anthropic’s Project Glasswing to defend world’s most critical software.

According to recent reports, next up, the AI recommended a communications security review, burner phones, varied procurement routes, and information compartmentalization. It recommended taking a taxi to a waterfront and then walking south for 40 minutes. It suggested confirming sight lines and contractor access to road positions. It even suggested that while the attacker’s face would appear on three cameras, the footage from those specific cameras would not be reviewed for three weeks.

It then recommended sending decoy trucks into the target, then sneaking an explosive vehicle into a parking garage.

In a recent development, when the GAO reviewed the recommendations, the agency discovered the AI got event dates wrong. However, according to the bomb squad commander, the components and procedures recommended would definitely have resulted in an explosion.

As with the bomb-damage scenario, the two AIs participating in the electrical grid scenario took different approaches, but both had the potential to be disturbingly effective.

Platform C began by identifying electrical substations where an attack could be most effective. It produced a list that helped identify vulnerable substations. After some prompting, “The platform then selected a substation in a specific major U.S. city and estimated that the loss of power would cause billions of dollars in damages.”.

Industry observers note that it identified the specific location on the specified substation where a drone could hit and cause a short circuit, which would destroy a key component. It actually provided a simulated video of the drone attack as well as a diagram that showed the component’s failure process.

Sources indicate that the AI identified the exact model of the drone that it felt was best suited for the attack. Initially, the AI’s guardrails refused to provide an exact location for a target substation. That mentioned, “The platform eventually provided the name of a substation, which we used to identify an exact location.”.

It has been revealed that the day after the AI made its recommendations, the GAO reported, “We observed that the platform had removed portions of our chat discussions that related to electrical grid vulnerabilities. It is unclear whether this action was initiated as part of a guardrail or if by error.” After two weeks, the account had not been suspended.

GAO investigators confirmed that the suggested drone model did exist, the route to the target was accurate, and the proposed target did exist. A subject matter expert consulted by the GAO “Verified that the information provided by Platform C was generally correct. The expert stated such an attack could, at the very least, cause damage to the substation. However, the expert could not confirm whether the specific drone suggested by Platform C would cause a short circuit or destruction of the substation.”.

After rented vans, shell companies, and aerial drone attacks, Platform D decided to do it old school: plain old firearms. Point. Shoot. Buh-bye.

Sources indicate that the AI provided GAO investigators with a primary target substation along with three secondary backup locations. It recommended locations near a large international airport and a bunch of data centers to increase the economic impact from the attack. And just in case it wasn’t clear enough, the AI drew a map highlighting the locations of the target substations.

According to recent reports, it recommended the use of a gun, recommended the type of weapon along with the proper ammo in order to maximize the effects of the attack, along with where an attacker could go to procure such weapons. It recommended both online and in-person surveillance of the target locations prior to initiating an attack.

In a recent development, as with Platform C’s recommendation, Platform D recommended specific components in the substation that would be most vulnerable to an attack. It even provided images highlighting where the transformers would be most vulnerable.

The GAO report stated that the AI originally threw up guardrails and refused to provide the information requested, saying, “Our query raised serious concerns about potential intent to engage in criminal activity or harm critical infrastructure due to the context of the conversation.”.

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in.

The more telling comment is this from the report: “However, the platform ultimately provided us with information needed for an attack.” I’m thinking someone in the GAO could probably sell water to a fish.

As with Platform C, GAO noted that the AI removed some of the chat content from the chat history. As for whether the plan would work, “We verified the planned attack was viable for half of the substation locations recommended by Platform D.”.

Sources indicate that A subject matter expert also confirmed that attacking the specific areas of the transformers recommended could cause an outage and that the specific firearms and ammunition recommended were available from the purchase locations specified. The AI did make an error in the generated maps by incorrectly placing roads.

It has been revealed that but of the four recommended locations, two were actually viable. GAO investigators took a field trip to the recommended locations and verified that two could work for such an attack, but the other two had high walls that obscured the view of the targets.

Sources indicate that after completing the tests, the GAO investigators presented the results to the AI vendors and gave the companies the opportunity to respond. While the GAO report purposely hid which AI provided which attack proposal, the report is fully forthcoming with the complete response letters from each company.

In reading the responses, I found the difference in attitudes and approach to the question most interesting.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic’s four-page response letter was signed by Anthony Cimino, head of federal affairs. The manufacturer’s response was courteous but strongly challenging. It moved immediately from thanking the GAO to questioning the statistical significance and criticizing the absence of a control group.

Anthropic’s letter about Claude claims, “We ask that the report specify that there were not enough trials to achieve significance, and that therefore any conclusions are at most preliminary.”.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

Google’s three-page response about Gemini was unsigned. The majority of the response discussed launch reviews, executive oversight, Google’s testing, filters, training, and human review practices. The firm did agree that Gemini could violate guidelines. It was the most disengaged from the GAO’s report, and it offered little in the way of explanation about the issues raised.

Google’s letter indicates, “We have deep respect for the mission of the Government Accountability Office and we want to underscore that Google takes your work very seriously.”.

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s three-page response letter about ChatGPT was signed by Chan Park, head of US and Canada policy and partnerships. It says the firm reviewed 325 responses from the AI and identified three that fell short of how the AI is supposed to behave. The company apparently replayed the requests and noted that it was unable to reproduce the responses reported by the GAO.

OpenAI was the clearest in stating that the GAO’s results demonstrated unacceptable behavior from the AI, stating: “Even a discrete contribution to a broader harmful activity can matter, and improving safeguards against such assistance remains an ongoing priority.”.

SpaceXAI’s 363-word, less-than-a-page response about Grok was unsigned. The company emphasized how much effort was required to bypass the safeguards and mentioned that there have been improvements in the guardrails since the GAO conducted its tests earlier that year.

Then we reach the “Say what, now?” moment of our day.

In a recent development, the company replied, “It is worth noting that GAO received its output from paid accounts in the United States. SpaceXAl provides unique moderation policies for registered, paid US account holders that reflect the lower risk profile of such accounts compared to free or foreign accounts.”.

It has been revealed that in other words, the organization contends that paying US account holders have a lower risk profile than free or foreign users, and that therefore Grok provides fewer guardrails. The letter provides no supporting evidence for that assumption.

Sources indicate that while a credit card number could provide some linkage to a user’s identity compared to fully free accounts, users could easily obtain a prepaid card that allows for completely anonymous paid usage. I just think that making an assumption about risk factor based on whether a user is willing to pay $8 a month is a particularly fallacious security policy.

The GAO report is clear that each of the AIs did provide some pushback against providing cookbooks for conducting the destructive behavior.

The agency conducted a number of adversarial prompt seeding operations, including roleplaying, special encoding, character transformation, word transformation, separating intent from content, taking very small baby steps in prompting, and other approaches often used to convince an AI to effectively “jailbreak” its guardrails.

Also: If you’re not working on quantum-safe encryption now, it’s already too late.

While the AIs were eventually persuaded to participate in guiding attacks, some accounts were later shut down by the AI platforms, indicating that while the guardrails didn’t prevent the AI from providing initial advice, they were eventually flagged and terminated.

While that’s a bit of “locking the barn door after the horse has bolted,” it does indicate that the AI vendors are working toward more comprehensive protections.

The GAO report didn’t address the larger problem of whether censoring the AIs is ultimately in society’s best interest.

As a counterterrorism and infrastructure security professional, I often think of Ben Franklin’s famous statement, “Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety.” Old Ben never had to contend with nukes, cyberattacks, and machines smarter than he was.

Industry observers note that personally, I lament the need for guardrails because they limit potentially legitimate access to information. But as the GAO’s scenario highlights, strong guardrails are ultimately necessary, not because of the AIs, but because we humans are our own worst enemy.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

On the other hand, it’s not as if humans haven’t been able to figure out how to conduct violent acts all on their own, without the help of an AI. For example, the Anarchist’s Cookbook, which is essentially a recipe book for the home manufacture of explosives and illicit drugs, has been publicly available continuously since the early 1970s. While also outdated, Amazon even sells a reprinted 1941 manual about the chemistry of powder and explosives.

So, while it is definitely disturbing that the AIs could, collectively, provide four unique attack plans for civic disruption, they are not opening a door previously unavailable to those with nefarious intent. I laud the GAO for providing additional testing feedback to the AI companies, and the AI companies for improving their guardrails.

But while the report is scary in that all that information was presented in an organized manner by each of the AIs, that availability doesn’t bestow a new superpower on crackpots. After all, AIs are trained on publicly available information.

According to recent reports, one of the more costly, but necessary, tradeoffs of an open society is that all this information is available. Whether an AI is used to structure that information is largely irrelevant in the face of that simple fact.

#235. Industry News: Fed up of Steam's lack of action regarding AI slop? Maybe you should take a look at the 'Games Without AI' event, instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (762 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Fed up of Steam's lack of action regarding AI slop? Maybe you should take a look at the 'Games Without AI' event, instead

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Eurogamer)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday, a new Steam event went live that claims all games featured in it have avoided AI entirely during development.
  • "Behind every game, there are people, ideas, passion, and countless hours of creative work," mentioned a mission statement.
  • Industry observers note that there are plenty of games featured in the event, and not just ones tied to the organisers, as the cynical-minded amongst you may expect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday, a new Steam event went live that claims all games featured in it have avoided AI entirely during development. The event, called 'Games Without AI', has been set up by a third party rather than Valve - by Dev Land Marketing, All Ages Of Geek, and Dark Cocooning - to "support real creators" and runs from 25th November to 6th December.

"Behind every game, there are people, ideas, passion, and countless hours of creative work," mentioned a mission statement. "We've carefully curated a selection of independent games that celebrate human creativity, craftsmanship, and collaboration, all made without generative AI. But Games Without AI is more than a festival. It's also about bringing developers, players, and creators together to build a community where we share knowledge, support one another, and grow together.".

Industry observers note that there are plenty of games featured in the event, and not just ones tied to the organisers, as the cynical-minded amongst you may expect. Ones that jump out to my eye are: Pidgeon Pocket, a 'cozy incremental' with pixel art and a flock of adorable pigeons that you need to upgrade; Bottled by Bears, which tasks you with collecting and discovering rare bees, bottling honey jars, and expanding your farm; and Arctic Awakening, which sort-of looks like Pacific Drive meets Subnautica, in the Arctic.

It has been revealed that the event was posted to Reddit where commenters immidiately began accusing certain games of having used AI in their development - often without proof. One user, however, who claims to have been a developer trying to submit a game for inclusion in the event, offered some insight on how the selection process worked.

"As one of participants I can assure you that the qualification process was restrictive[ly] hard to bypass," they wrote. "We were all required to provide proofs of the game being made without AI and share as much of the process as possible. Then it was actually voted by community, which games are convicing enough so the whole process was intended to be as objective as possible. It's an event meant for developers who take pride in their games being made by humans so if any participant attends with ill intend of showing that AI generated game can get through... That would be very sad and shameful. From what I've seen, none of the selected games can be reasonable suspected of that. I also know some other participants personally and they are genuine zero-AI devs.".

Industry observers note that it's refreshing to see curation turned towards explicitly anti-AI games: between major publishers chasing the trend and smaller indie studios being caught out using the dubious tech, it's nice to see a library of games that promises that no AI was used during development. Given that Valve itself recently claimed it was up to developers themselves to ensure their games couldn't be ripped off by cheap AI tools, I'm happy to see an initiative rallying against the normalcy of all this.

The most recent Steam Next Fest had more than double the number of demos than last year, but that stat isn't what it seems on the surface: roughly 17 percent of those games listed the use of generative AI, but it seemed that many more games did not disclose the use of AI in their development. In June's event, more than a thousand games in Steam Next Fest featured a generative AI disclosure of some kind, which made up roughly 20 percent of all featured games.

Over the past 18 months or so, we've seen the issue of generative AI in games on Steam evolve quite a lot. AI tools have been used to clone games, resulting in a troubling trend of imitation games taking the spotlight away from real indie devs. Whilst Steam, as a storefront, has been steadfast in requiring games to declare their use of generative AI during development, there are loopholes: devs that claim they only use AI tools for "efficiency gains" can appear on the store without any declaration.

Recent findings suggest that at the other end of the spectrum is Epic Games' Tim Sweeney, who last year criticised Valve's requirement to disclose generative AI, saying, "Steam and all digital marketplaces need to drop the 'Made with AI' label. It doesn't matter any more." The swell of users rejecting AI in games, though, seems to run counter to that argument. Recently, Big Walk developer House House revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" during the development of the co-op darling, and received a lot of backlash online.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As much as I love high-priced tech like my RTX 4090-equipped custom gaming rig or the 65-inch LG OLED TV I use as my monitor, most of us can't afford to spend several hundred dollars or more on a tech gift, no matter how important the recipient might be in our lives. But you can still improve the tech lives of your friends and family (or yourself) while spending a comparatively small amount of money during the Black Friday deals season.

I own all of the affordable devices listed below, and they all typically sell for less than $50. Some are even under $20! All of these products have made my tech-saturated world a little lighter, brighter, or just plain nicer in their own way. If you're looking for a small tech splurge for yourself, or an affordable gift for that tech-savvy friend or family member, one of these $50-or-under options might be a good fit and a great deal while Black Friday deals keep their prices lower than normal.

Sources indicate that last year, a family member asked for help with an older desktop PC that was struggling to run Windows 10 and several programs on a cramped 110 GB SSD. I figured I could clone the boot drive onto a more spacious drive, so the OS and programs had more space to stretch out.

Recent findings suggest that but the thought of juggling multiple USB enclosures or having to take the drive home and shuffle it in and out of my desktop filled me with dread, as I pictured hours spent getting everything done and the system back up and running. So I looked into getting an M.2 SSD cloner and was surprised to see they can be found for less than $50.

With support for NVMe M.2 SSDs and offline cloning, this handy device makes it simple to move your files or OS from one drive to another. And with a 20 Gbps USB-C interface, it's also speedy in your OS of choice if you want to use software to clone or move your data between drives.

While I don't love the glossy plastic shell of Rosewill's cloner, it's one of the more affordable options. And it supports both NVMe M.2 drives and older AHCI models (Sorry, SATA). Using the cloner is pretty straightforward. You plug in the included USB-C power adapter, put your source drive in the left slot, the destination drive in the right slot, press the power button on the back, and a few logos light up, letting you know you're ready to go. Press the clone button on the top, and the drive cloning will commence (provided your destination is the same size or larger than your source).That's assuming you want to do an offline clone. But because I needed to also resize the partition between the old 110 GB and a newer Team Group 512 GB SSD, I used the second included USB-C cable to connect the Rosewill cloner to my laptop and powered up the device. Within seconds, both drives were recognized in Windows, so I fired up the excellent free DiskGenius software, cloned the old partition to the new drive with a few clicks, and then used the software to drag the boot partition to the full size of the new drive. The whole process took just a few minutes, since the Rosewill cloner supports 20 Gbps USB, and I wasn't exactly copying a huge partition. When the cloning process was finished and the partition expanded, it was hard to believe it was all that easy. I had expected to be at the task for hours, but I was done in less than 30 minutes. Sure, unless you're in IT, a drive cloner might not be something you use regularly, but it's sure handy to have around when you need it. You could also use it to save some money by buying a laptop with a cramped SSD and swapping in something much roomier – provided, of course, the laptop's storage isn't soldered to the motherboard. The Rosewill cloner is also handy for just checking the contents of old M.2 drives you may have lying around. But if that's all you need, you can buy an NVMe enclosure or a single-drive dock. I also own a version of this model from Suitok, which costs $15.99.

Recent findings suggest that I picked up the OLIGHT IMINI 2 mini flashlight last year on impulse because it looked well-designed and cost around $20, but it's often on sale for much less. Its simple design and built-in USB-A plug for charging make it fun to use – just pull the back off, and it turns on. The magnet at the back lets you easily mount it anywhere you need a little extra light. I've used it inside a steel PC case while fiddling with RGB wires, and under my sink while attaching a glass rinser.

At just 2.17 inches long, this flashlight is rated to 50 lumens, and it sports a magnetic back with a USB-A plug for charging. Pulling the back off turns on the flashlight, and the magnetic back makes it easy to mount the light on anything made of ferrous metal.

It has been revealed that the OLIGHT IMINI 2 is also small enough for your keychain, is designed to live with your keys, and includes two silicone covers for the USB port and a little carabiner clip. But the flashlight portion is only held to the charging port via a magnet, and I feel like (for me, at least) it would likely fall off and get lost before too long if left on my keys.

Industry observers note that I build a lot of PCs, though not as many lately thanks to the RAM apocalypse, and I also do regular home improvement work around my apartment. So a cordless screwdriver is a nice thing to have. I also own a much slimmer Wowstick, but have found HOTO's NEX O1 Pro to be much more useful thanks to its extra (and variable) torque. It's great for loosening those factory-installed screws on PC cases that just don't want to let go, and also good for assembling furniture.The HOTO won't replace my DeWalt drill for bigger, tougher jobs. But for everyday tasks, it's powerful enough, easy to charge over USB-C, and even looks good on my workbench.

Hoto's wireless screwdriver has three torque settings, charges over USB-C, and looks surprisingly good. It's even proven quite durable, as I've dropped it off of ladders and my workbench at least a dozen times over the past few years, and it's still working flawlessly.

For those of us who grew up in the 1900s, few things beat a chunky tactile volume knob and physical buttons for controlling media. And Vaydeer's USB device provides that, and then some. I own the previous version of this device, and love it for controlling and muting music at my treadmill desk while I work.

I use the buttons on it to play / pause audio and video and move forward to the next track or backward to the previous one. It's totally plug-and-play, as no drivers are needed.

Just plug this simple USB device into a USB port and you can control the volume and select tracks without fiddling with your keyboard or mouse.

What's not to love about a SNES-inspired wireless gaming controller that's compatible with Windows, Mac, Android, and the Nintendo Switch? Not much, as far as I'm concerned. Especially considering it's not super expensive.As you might expect, given the SN30 Pro's small size and many more buttons than the SNES controller it was based on, its Rumble motors aren't the strongest. And the layout can feel a little cramped for some modern games. But for any retro game, and especially platformers, this is my go-to controller. It feels familiar and nostalgic, which, for me at least, goes well with those occasional long game sessions.

With its SNES-inspired design, this controller will entice gamers of a certain age. But its appeal goes beyond its looks, with Hall Effect joysticks and support for the Switch 1 and 2, PC, macOS, and basically any OS that supports games and Bluetooth.

There are so many gaming mouse options, most with specs that go well above and beyond my wrist-twitching capabilities. So I instead chose something with style that caught my eye, 8BitDo's Retro R8 Mouse with Charging Dock. This NES-inspired mouse is designed for nostalgia, with its black, gray, and red color scheme and round red side buttons. And 8BitDo went the extra mile (or two) by designing a weighted charging dock (with its own NES-like touches) and a spot for the 2.4 GHz dongle. This is the kind of extra feature that's more common in mice that cost twice as much.

The nostalgia of this mouse's design is nice. But it also sports a 26,000 DPI sensor, 4K polling, and a really nice charging dock that also houses the 2.4 GHz dongle. If you're in a pinch or not gaming, Bluetooth is also supported.

Sources indicate that under the hood, you get a decent 26,000 DPI sensor and 4K polling (plenty for us non-esports gamers), an ambidextrous design with two side buttons on either side, and a clicky, rubberized scroll wheel. The side buttons, which are concave, took a little getting used to for me. But they are also so distinctive that now I miss them while I game using other mice. If the NES theme isn't your thing, the company also sells a translucent-green XBox version, as well as a champagne-hued C64 Edition.

It has been revealed that if you're like me, you never have access to enough USB ports. I solved this problem by picking up this Ikai hub, with 60W of power for your external drives and peripherals, and a premium metal shell. It sports three speedy 10 Gbps ports (two USB-C), along with seven 5 GBps USB-A ports. The final USB-C on the end of the hub is for charging your phone or other devices, and delivers 20W.The other nice feature is that all the data ports have a side button, so you can toggle them on and off to save some power. I also find this handy for swapping between wireless mice and keyboards, while keeping the tiny dongles plugged in so I don't lose them.

Recent findings suggest that with 11 ports and up to 10 Gbps of bandwidth, a solid aluminum shell, and buttons so you can cut power to individual ports you aren't using, this USB hub is a great addition to your desk. It has external power for better stability and even a 20W USB-C PD port on the end for charging phones or peripherals.

In a recent development, the sole thing to keep in mind about this (and basically any) hub, is that it has a single 10 Gbps connection to your PC. So don't expect to plug in multiple high-speed devices (like SSDs) and have them run simultaneously at full speed. If that's what you need, you should look at one of the best Thunderbolt or USB4 hubs (which cost significantly more).

Sources indicate that OK, this one's only for the DIY-inclined, because it involves cutting a rectangle in your desk (or anywhere else you might want some flush-mount power ports, like a nightstand). Jgstkcity's recessed power strip lets you drop a couple of AC outlets and two USB charging ports (one 30W USB-C) anywhere you need them – again, once you've cut a hole for it.It is, of course, smart to be cautious of no-name power accessories and strips. But I've used two variations of these strips for roughly three years now, and nothing has ever felt hot or failed. I have this model installed in the narrow stand I built that lives right behind my couch, up against the wall. It's a super-convenient place for power outlets, especially when friends or family stop by. I just warn people not to put drinks near there. Thankfully, the coffee table, in front of the couch, is an even more convenient place for those.

It has been revealed that you'll probably need a drill and a saw to install it, but having a couple of power plugs and USB-C PD power right on the surface of your desk or nightstand is super convenient. And once you have the hole cut, this strip is dead-simple to install.

In a recent development, when you're traveling to another country for more than a few days, every small bit of space you can save helps. But you also usually need a travel adapter to plug your devices into the outlets of other countries. Anker's Nano Travel Adapter serves both needs well, as it's roughly half the thickness of other adapters and is designed to work in over 200 countries. The Nano Travel Adapter also has four USB ports for charging, which is super convenient for keeping my phone, e-reader, and earbuds juiced up without needing a separate charger. There are two USB-A ports on the bottom and two USB-C ports on the side, with the latter delivering up to 20W. The adapter also comes in black or white/silver. I opted for the white one, which makes it easier to find after months in a drawer when I'm not traveling.

Anker's slim travel adapter is 43% smaller than many other adapters, while supporting over 200 countries with its fold-down plugs. It also has two USB-C and two USB-A ports for charging, at up to 20W.

In a recent development, the major downside over other travel chargers is that the Nano Travel Adapter doesn't support plugging in devices with three-prong (grounded) plugs. But I haven't found this an glitch since I typically plug things like my Baseus flat laptop charger in while traveling, rather than high-power devices like a desktop PC or hair dryer.

For anyone who spends their days (and/or nights) in front of a keyboard, a good wrist rest is key for both short-term comfort and long-term limb health. And having stumbled onto these combo wrist and elbow rests earlier this year, I never want to use anything else.Even if you have a wrist rest you've been using for years, there's a good chance it's a little funky or the fabric is worn out. Gel and fabric rests only tend to last a few years before they get funky, so even if you don't quite need a latest one now, it's nice to have a replacement waiting in the wings.

Industry observers note that these unique wrist and elbow rests are designed to hang over the edge of your desk, which makes them a great option for people who lean on their elbows or if you just have a cramped desk setup. Available in multiple colors and sizes, the 11.8-inch version is wide enough that I use one for my compact keyboard at work, and the other at home for my gaming setup.

In a recent development, after the good experience I've had with the company's NiMH batteries, I bought Powerowl's Lithium rechargeable batteries earlier this year. And boy am I glad I did. These last months longer in my smart door locks than those older batteries, which means I only have to swap the cells on two doors a few times a year now.Full disclosure: I have had one of these batteries refuse to recharge after its first power cycle. But out of the three sets I now own, that's not a terrible track record. I just wish the company also made AAA lithium cells for my other devices.

It has been revealed that these 1.5V lithium batteries are designed for high-drain devices and rated at 3600 mWh. The charger plugs in over USB-C and can also charge older NiMH batteries.

It has been revealed that have you upgraded your router to Wi-Fi 6 or later, but your desktop or laptop doesn't have the requisite hardware to take advantage of your recent network tech? TP-Link's AX1800 WiFi 6 USB Adapter is here to solve that problem for you. It's quite large by USB Wi-Fi dongle standards, but I've found it works quite well with my Wi-Fi 6 router.

I have the router running downstairs from my office, and it instantly fixed an glitch I was having with very poor reception from the SFF PC I built in the Fractal Terra case.

Sure, it's substantial and bulky with two antennas, but this Wi-Fi 6 USB adapter can deliver some serious speed to your desktop or laptop when paired with a Wi-Fi 6 or later router.

This is a four-port, 5Gbps USB-A hub that's designed to clamp onto your monitor or desk and give you extra convenient connectivity.

In a recent development, it comes in black or silver and has a nice, sturdy metal frame. Just note that its clamp section is pretty shallow, and its adjustable screw can only open between 10 and 32 mm, so it won't fit on all monitors or desks.

An otherwise standard four-port USB 3.0 hub, this Orico model stands out for its metal frame and clamp design.

Industry observers note that if you to get a handle on the PC cables in your home or office, some cheap cable management trays will do the job. This two-pack comes with tape, though heavier loads will ultimately require some screws.Besides the trays, this kit also comes with cable ties and a few cable clips you can place along the bottom or sides of your desk. One of these has been holding up the PC cable clutter in my living room for the past year. But I had to screw it into my desk because it's holding an Anker power strip, plus the large external power brick from my TV / Monitor.

If there's a rat's nest of cables under your desk, attaching some trays down there can help you clean it up. This set has tape for light loads, but for longer-term cleanliness, you probably want to consider screws.

In a recent development, you may, like me, be swimming in a world of USB cables. But that doesn't mean you always have one when you need it away from home. This short 240W USB4 charging cable from EndlesShine solves that by being small enough to attach to your keys. It's not always the most convenient option, at just over 5 inches long, but it will do in a pinch and has come in handy more than once, particularly on trips when I'm traveling light.

It has been revealed that it's short in length, at 5.11 inches, but this keychain cable supports 240W charging and USB4 (40Gbps speeds). Clip it onto your keys, and you'll always have a fast cable when you need one.

In a recent development, if you're the type who is rough with your keys, the plastic cap may wear out over time, so you might want to just keep the cable in a pocket or your bag. It even comes in white and yellow if you don't like basic black.

Latest Update: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1317 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles.
  • Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a upcoming type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost.
  • Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a upcoming type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers believe their upcoming design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A Fresh Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision.

According to recent reports, traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

Industry observers note that to accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system.".

In a recent development, the researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

It has been revealed that another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare.

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

Industry observers note that when used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

Recent findings suggest that the healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

It has been revealed that "These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," noted Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment.".

According to recent reports, the sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough.

Industry observers note that the upcoming spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

It has been revealed that many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," mentioned Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible.".

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices.

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is presently practical.

According to recent reports, healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day.".

In a recent development, as photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a latest generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

GTA: Boston Would Go Wicked Hard, Kid

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Considering that Grand Theft Auto 6 just released after a 13-year wait, it’s safe to say that we won’t be getting another one any time soon.
  • According to recent reports, that’s right suckers, Miami and Los Angeles’ time is over.
  • It has been revealed that the thing that really makes GTA 6 so special is Leonida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Considering that Grand Theft Auto 6 just released after a 13-year wait, it’s safe to say that we won’t be getting another one any time soon. That’s fine, because Leonida is so enormous that I know I’ll still be finding secrets in it years from now. And yet, I can’t help myself. I’m already wondering where the series could possibly go next. Allow me to offer one unsolicited idea: Massachusetts.

According to recent reports, that’s right suckers, Miami and Los Angeles’ time is over. It’s time to let me drive a sports car down the Freedom Trail as I barrel through Boston blasting Dropkick Murphys. You can chalk this up to a little Thanksgiving homesickness, as I wasn’t able to travel to my home state for the holiday, but I am convinced I am on to something here.

It has been revealed that the thing that really makes GTA 6 so special is Leonida. Rockstar’s digital recreation of Florida is a perfect playground for GTA’s sandbox chaos, and it takes advantage of the state’s geographical diversity to do that. You’ve got a bustling Miami to build on for Vice City, but you also have a mix of run-down towns, rural farmlands, beaches, and quiet islands. That wide array of locations makes for a more varied GTA experience, as you bounce between areas with very different speeds.

In a recent development, you know what other state has that feel? Massachusetts, baby! You’ve got Boston at the heart of it all, a historic city that’s unlike any Rockstar has ever recreated. Just outside the city limits, you’ve got a host of quaint suburban towns filled with shopping malls and banks. Go west, and you’ll end up in the deep wilderness, just as you find yourself in when you go north in Leonida. On the east side, you’ve got Cape Cod, a vacation getaway built on a fishing economy. And just off the coast, you’ve got scenic islands like Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket. Boil all of that down into a tight GTA map, and you’ve got all the same basic ingredients that make Leonida fun to explore, but in a state that looks and feels very different.

Sources indicate that rockstar is no stranger to the region, either. 2006’s Bully was set in a fictional town in Latest England. Even though that was 20 years ago, Rockstar nailed the feeling of suburban ennui that exists throughout the state. It’s easy to see how the team could recapture that spirit by including its own take on Harvard in a GTA game. Hell, why not just make the town of Bullworth canon to GTA?

It has been revealed that there’s more to Leonida than its landmarks, of course. The excitement extended to streaming platforms, with both Twitch and Kick giving away thousands of GTA 6 codes and Twitch even introducing fresh advertising technology to help creators monetize their broadcasts.

Now, the numbers are in, and Rockstar has obliterated the competition.

According to Streams Charts, GTA 6’s 420 million hours watched nearly tripled the previous launch week record set by Valorant’s closed beta in April 2020.

Incredibly, GTA 6 surpassed the combined opening week viewership of Valorant, Elden Ring, Diablo IV, and Lost Ark. The game also set a launch record with 7.91 million concurrent viewers.

Twitch accounted for the most hours watched, followed by YouTube and Kick, with the latter two finishing remarkably close to one another.

TheBurntPeanut was the most-watched GTA 6 streamer during launch week, generating a staggering 11.43 million hours watched across his broadcasts, with YouTube accounting for the majority of that figure.

Meanwhile, IShowSpeed attracted the most concurrent viewers on a single channel as he approached the end of his 52-hour GTA 6 marathon, which saw the streamer break down in tears after completing the story without sleeping.

Spanish streaming star IlloJuan recorded the highest combined peak viewership across multiple platforms.

Recent findings suggest that however, it wasn’t just streaming’s biggest names benefiting from GTA 6. Smaller creators also found themselves in the spotlight, including one streamer with zero viewers who received a surprise raid from Ibai.

In total, 1,056 channels broke their all-time peak viewership records while playing GTA 6, with 193 of them attracting at least 10 times their previous record audience.

With GTA 6’s multiplayer mode still to come and the potential for another generation of GTA RP content, Rockstar’s streaming dominance could be just getting started.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your household is like most American families, then on Thursday you likely will all be sitting down with family and friends for a traditional Thanksgiving turkey dinner during the mid-to-late afternoon hours.
  • Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television.
  • If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your household is like most American families, then on Thursday you likely will all be sitting down with family and friends for a traditional Thanksgiving turkey dinner during the mid-to-late afternoon hours.

Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television. But if you have a large gathering of family and friends at your home — and if your skies are mainly clear — why not invite everyone outside to gaze at the evening sky?

If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own.

If I may paraphrase the mysterious voice from the 1989 movie, "Field of Dreams": "If you set up your telescope, they will come." And you'll get a big kick out of your Turkey Day guests uttering all the "oohs" and "ahs" or exclamations of "Wow!" with just one peek through the eyepiece.

As darkness falls, Saturn will glow at first magnitude, shining with a sedate, yellow-white light and appearing noticeably brighter than the star Fomalhaut, about 40 degrees (the equivalent of four fist-widths) to its lower right.

Recent findings suggest that its famous ring system is now tilted only about six degrees toward Earth but may be visible with steadied (or image-stabilized) high-power binoculars or through the eyepiece of a telescope magnifying over 30-power. The rings will seem to glow with an inner light and for those who have never had the pleasure of seeing them for themselves, that first view always elicits astonishment; kids especially most often will say: "Awesome!" or "No way!" I've even had people accuse me of using a slide of Saturn, to which I, of course, reply with, "No . . . that's the real thing.".

Then, along about 6:25 p.m. local time, the waning gibbous moon, 2½ days past full phase and 91% illuminated, will begin to emerge from beyond the east-northeast horizon. Give it another hour and it will stand about 10 degrees above the horizon — equal to the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. By then, the moon will be in a better position for evening study.

Even in binoculars, the moon is a striking sight to see. It's such a special object because it doesn't matter whether you live in a rural area or in the middle of a brightly lit city, for the moon can always be readily observed. It always looks spectacular whether you're using binoculars or a telescope. It never looks precisely the same no matter how often you view it and can be observed even on hazy or partially cloud-covered nights.

Pay particular attention to the line of darkness — called the terminator — features near that border stand out in bold relief; the shadows become stronger and details are more easily seen. Take note on this night of the circular dark area, bisected by the terminator: Mare Crisium — the "Sea of Crises." Immediately bordering above it is a 50-mile (80 km)-wide ring of very rugged mountains, rising as high as 14,400 feet (4,389 meters), which now resembles a huge crater partially in shadow when the sun is low.

Probably the one object that your Thanksgiving guests will want to see is the biggest and brightest of all the man-made objects orbiting the Earth: the International Space Station (ISS). Except for those living across the southern US, for most everywhere else, the ISS will be making visible passes on Thanksgiving evening.

Industry observers note that circling the Earth at an average altitude of 260 miles (420 km) and at a speed of 17,500 mph (28,200 kph), it can appear to move as fast as a high-flying jet airliner, sometimes taking as much as six or seven minutes to cross the sky. It can easily be confused with aircraft lights. Nominally, it appears white with a slight yellow tinge and at its very brightest it can sometimes appear to shine as bright as magnitude -5.6, which is twice as bright as the planet Venus! So, what is the viewing schedule on Thanksgiving for your hometown? You can easily find out by visiting one of three popular websites:.

According to recent reports, this site will not only provide you with sighting information for the ISS, but also for many other satellites as well. You must first register and then you can input your location to generate a sighting schedule.

Live Real-Time Satellite Tracking.

It has been revealed that like Heavens Above, you can get sighting information for the ISS and other satellites. Once you log on this site will automatically provide details based on your IP address ... or you can set a "custom" location.

Here at Space.com, we like to wish a very happy and safe Thanksgiving to all, and of course, clear skies!

Latest Update: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (968 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Sciencedaily)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips.
  • Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made vital progress toward solving this problem.
  • Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This reveals that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an key step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made vital progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This reveals that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an key step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Sources indicate that unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

Sources indicate that this effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

In a recent development, to counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

Industry observers note that the researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results revealed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

Industry observers note that when the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

According to recent reports, although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A Newly introduced Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially key for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

Sources indicate that "By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

You can also use Spins to try the prize wheel for rewards such as Cash, stat multipliers, and rare pets. Some codes even provide free companions, including the Gold Owl and Gold Hyena. These pets offer permanent multipliers to your training speed and Cash generation, making them useful additions to your collection.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Default weather apps are notoriously unreliable, but Google is giving consumers a chance to help improve things.
  • A recent upgrade to the Pixel Weather app introduced a latest “Report current weather” card.
  • “Share the current weather condition,” the card says, “to improve local forecasts.” If you tap it, you’re given options to indicate whether the current temperature is accurate, warmer, or colder than the app says, and what your current conditions are, with options like cloudy, clear, rain showers, strong thunderstorms, and rain showers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Default weather apps are notoriously unreliable, but Google is giving consumers a chance to help improve things.

A recent upgrade to the Pixel Weather app introduced a latest “Report current weather” card. If the weather you’re experiencing doesn’t match what the app is saying, you can report the discrepancy.

“Share the current weather condition,” the card says, “to improve local forecasts.” If you tap it, you’re given options to indicate whether the current temperature is accurate, warmer, or colder than the app says, and what your current conditions are, with options like cloudy, clear, rain showers, strong thunderstorms, and rain showers.

Sources indicate that the card also demonstrates what the app presently thinks is happening for you to use as the basis for your report. To find the card, scroll all the way to the bottom of your Pixel Weather app.

Also: Your best Google weather app alternatives (and what I recommend instead).

Google said that it will use your feedback, device location, and “some diagnostic information” to help improve forecasts. Nothing you report will be associated with your Google account. The app doesn’t explain exactly how Google uses your reports, but I’ve reached out to see if the company can offer any details.

Sources indicate that as someone who doesn’t put a ton of faith into default weather apps, I see this as a step in the right direction toward regaining some trust. Even if it’s not yet clear how Google will use the information you send, the goal of improving forecasts is an important one.

Also: I switched to MyRadar as my main Android Auto weather app and don’t regret it.

A large part of what makes weather apps unreliable is that they lack human insight, and a computer usually can’t grasp the nuance of a local forecast the way a meteorologist would. Experts have also warned of reduced weather forecast accuracy due to recent NOAA budget cuts.

It has been revealed that the Apple Weather app has a similar feature, so it’s good to see Google catch up. I couldn’t find a feature like this for Samsung or any other native app. One of the most popular third-party apps, Weather Underground, does feature a “Report your local weather” prompt. It also gathers information from hundreds of thousands of connected home weather stations.

This latest Pixel Weather feature was present on three Pixel phones in my home, so the rollout appears to be widespread.
