#221. Latest Update: "I'm betting on the sickos" - Signet City intends to 'expand the scope of RPGs' by drawing on the success of Citizen Sleeper

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2508 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Eurogamer ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: "I'm betting on the sickos" - Signet City intends to 'expand the scope of RPGs' by drawing on the success of Citizen Sleeper

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
🎬 5-Second Live Source Screen Capture (Eurogamer)
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I last spoke to Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin, it was on the eve of Citizen Sleeper 2's release.
  • "I feel a certain responsibility that comes with success," Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - told me at the time.
  • They wanted the definition of RPGs to be "expanded", to make them as varied as "rich and varied" as tabletop RPGs can be.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I last spoke to Citizen Sleeper creator Gareth Damian Martin, it was on the eve of Citizen Sleeper 2's release. Like its predecessor, the game was a critical hit, cementing Damian Martin's reputation as one of the most successful independent game developers around. But they weren't content. They wanted to do more, to push more, to stretch the idea of what a role-playing video game could be.

"I feel a certain responsibility that comes with success," Damian Martin - also known by their studio name Jump Over the Age - told me at the time. "I feel lots of things about this medium, and I feel if I'm in the one percent of indie developers - and the even smaller percent of solo developers - who manage to make something and have that thing be successful, then I have responsibility towards putting things into the industry and into the world that contribute somehow to whatever I think the industry should be doing.".

They wanted the definition of RPGs to be "expanded", to make them as varied as "rich and varied" as tabletop RPGs can be. Citizen Sleeper was a step towards realising that goal but even it had limitations, which is why Damian Martin has returned to take things a step further with their next game Signet City. Confirmed during this year's somewhat samey-feeling Summer Game Fest, it's a startlingly original work.

Signet City was enigmatic. Revealed in a cinematic trailer, it was black and white, bleak, thick-lined, smoggy, and dirty; choked in industrial decay and brimming with post-punk non-conformance. It was also first-person, a notable change for Damian Martin, whose games have, up until now, been zoomed out and abstracted. Most eye-catching of all, though, was the descriptor "fungalpunk" - a game in which we'd play as a parasite in someone's mind. As far as expanding the scope of RPGs goes: "100 percent that is exactly what I'm trying to do here," Gareth Damian Martin tells me now.

Industry observers note that we talk in a video call in the immediate aftermath of Signet City's announcement - apologies for not writing this until Not-GTA Week, though what an opportunity that presented - and Damian Martin is as calm and eloquent and thoughtful as ever, nestled in a compact office decorated with collages of their current influences. This room looked different when we spoke about Citizen Sleeper 1, looked different when we spoke about Citizen Sleeper 2, and it looks different again now. Damian Martin is a visual person, as someone with a visual design background would be.

With Signet City only just revealed, questions abound. The announcement trailer doesn't reveal much (not much has come out since, either), but we do know it takes place in the North of England in the 80s. It's a setting I'm not sure we've ever had in games, and one that's woefully overlooked in entertainment in general, barring BBC TV shows like Our Friends in the North and Boys from the Blackstuff, which Damian Martin directly references. We know there are themes like industrial decay, welded as they are to that time and place. But there's been no talk of how the game plays, or what being a parasite in someone's mind means.

After speaking with Damian Martin, I've got a much better idea. But first, to the beginning. Signet City is an idea they've had floating around their head for a very long time. This was the game they pitched to their publisher Fellow Traveller after Citizen Sleeper 1 came out, but decided to hold in favour of making Citizen Sleeper 2 - a decision driven partly by a desire "to build myself a bigger platform" to launch a upcoming game idea from. The idea originated in a very unexpected place: the musician Sting. Damian Martin was doing theatre design for Sting's musical show The Last Ship before they became a full-time game-maker (go back even further in Damian Martin's life and you'll find a degree in puppetry there). They had to research Newcastle in the 1980s because of it. The Last Ship is about Sting's upbringing in Wallsend, a town near Newcastle, in the wake of a shipyard being closed there - the town's source of sustenance. And it was while working on the project that the 80s imprinted on Damian Martin's mind.

"I was looking at these pictures of these massive gleaming ships hanging over the top of little terraced houses," they say, "and this conflict between time periods and ideas of society, and I remember thinking at the time: that was science-fiction somehow. When you look at those images, it could be a spaceship; that ship that's being built in Newcastle might as well be a spaceship, especially science-fiction of the 80s - a lot of it was about that.

Industry observers note that "It just stuck in my brain and I started to work up this fictional 1980s British city that would be in that period of de-industrialisation and social change," they continue. "But would be based on a completely different kind of industrial background and have this weird kind of fungalpunk technology layered into it. So that's been sitting around in my head for almost 10 years slowly accruing material and reference points and things.".

In a recent development, fungalpunk: there's that word again, but what does it mean? I've heard of cyberpunk and steampunk, not that I could tell you easily what they mean, but I've never heard of fungapunk - I don't think anyone has. Thankfully, in this case, it's fairly literal. "You are fungal in a very true sense," Damian Martin states. You are a fungal parasite and there are themes of decay and reinvigoration, things fungi are closely tied to. One of the phrases Damian Martin has been using as a north star for the project - something they do on all of their projects - is the idea of being "a fungal superhero", which makes me giggle. I've definitely not heard that before either.

In a recent development, it's an idea inspired by a 1989 Japanese film called Tetsuo: The Iron Man - about a salary man who's slowly turning into metal - that Damian Martin adores. "I love it so much," they say. "It's an amazing movie, a beautiful movie, and really strange. And so I wanted to do something that was in that vibe. The way that that film commits to the idea of a body becoming metal and the visceral kind of strangeness of that. I wanted to do something that was about humans and becoming fungal; which we already are, we already have lots of bits of bacteria and fungal nail infections - we are multitudes.".

It has been revealed that the punk side of the equation is, again, fairly literal. It refers to the post-punk cultural and musical scene at the time. The scene is often overshadowed by the brasher, more aggressive punk movement, but it's one that's just as anti-establishment, albeit in perhaps in a deeper, darker, more nihilistic way. Think Joy Division referencing novelist JG Ballard in its songs, for example. "Post-punk was this engagement with structural politics and transgressive fiction and all kinds of interesting major ideas getting into pop culture through music," Damian Martin indicates.

Recent findings suggest that now watch the game's trailer again; you can feel all these things oozing through it. The aesthetic, the music, the setting. There are also significant clues - although they're not obvious - about how the game plays. We see the start of a character called Sid's story in the trailer, who's one of the hosts we can inhabit in the game. We choose an area of the city we want to play in, then drop into a person's head who lives or operates there. And in Sid's case, she wakes up in a river just as we - the parasite - wake in her mind. Twins!

We control Sid as we would a character in another first-person game - Dishonored or Skyrim are two examples Damian Martin uses - and we see a bit of this in the trailer. What we don't see are any other mechanics, which are, once more, dice rolls related to skills, as in Citizen Sleeper. In order to do something in the world that isn't insignificantly easy, we need to roll a dice and add modifiers to see if we can achieve it.

"So the way it works is you drop into someone's head for the day. Let's say we drop into this worker's head for the day and we want to get to a certain part of the city, and let's say we need to kick down a door to get there," states Damian Martin. "Well, we're going to have to make this character really angry to get them to kick down that door, so we're going to maybe get them in an argument with some other fellow workers, and maybe we're going to choose to provoke that argument and then they'll get really angry. Then that will have narrative effects, but also it will have mechanical effects in the sense of, like, okay, now we have a modifier that makes physical strength more powerful, so we can do these physical strength actions.".

Skills are tied to a person's emotions, intriguingly, and your job as the parasite is to find things that affect these emotions so you can amplify them and increase your chances of achieving things. Then at the end of the day, all of that emotion gets "extracted out" and becomes a resource you can permanently improve your host's skills with. "So you start to adjust each of your hosts in a direction you think will be helpful for you to do what you need each day in these hub locations," Damian Martin explains. But this has consequences. Push someone towards angry actions and they'll become a more angry person, understandably. "And that will shape their future even when you're no longer controlling them.".

Which begs the question: what exactly does a parasite need to do? What is a parasite's objective in the game? This is an answer Damian Martin isn't quite ready to give, though they do their best to attempt it. "You have your own objectives as a parasite," they say. "You don't have an objective like: this is your mission, parasite. But there are some bigger offers coming to you through your sensorium, through your experience of voices and attractions and tastes and smells, that are leading you in different places as a parasite. That's your objective, to grow and gain power, although to what end you don't initially know.".

It's in this parasitical difference Signet City starts to stand apart. For starters, it's just appealing weird to be a parasite, though as Damian Martin muses, aren't we often parasites in relation to characters in tabletop role-playing games? "We push them around; sometimes we talk for them and sometimes we listen to them; sometimes we use our name and sometimes we use their name." Here, it's simply out in the open. "I wanted to create an RPG where I acknowledged and then also played that into the fiction," they say.

Recent findings suggest that being in a thing in someone's mind allows a host character autonomy, to a degree, so they can have their own motivations and stories and struggles besides yours. They don't have to be thoughtless mannequins awaiting our direction. Dropping into their minds allows us to drop straight into a tense scenario. "Stories for me that are very exciting in fiction and literature are stories about people who are in it," Damian Martin claims. "They're in the situation already, they're in the shit, they're having to deal with everything.".

The ability to read their minds also lets us know them more intimately than we know characters in other games, who usually, you know, need to speak to us in order for us to understand them. It also circumvents the need for an NPC to suddenly and unnaturally open up to you about their lives, the first moment they meet you, and to provide you with "a neatly packaged challenge". That's not needed here. "The core relationships of the game are actually between you and your hosts," Damian Martin notes.

In a recent development, there's a layer that exists on top of the character's thoughts where the parasite lives and functions - a layer of feelings and emotions and sensory reactions to a world outside. A hopefully quite bizarre and alien layer, which presents challenges of its own, because how do you describe the experiences of a parasite in someone's mind? "What does it feel like to be a parasite and how do I make that comprehensible to a human?" Damian Martin wonders. They are good questions I can't wait to experience the answers to.

Recent findings suggest that but when will that be? There's no release date yet, and when we talked in the summer, Signet City was only halfway through development. It was declared early partly to make sure people understood it wasn't Citizen Sleeper 3, and partly because people could probably use some time to sit with the idea for a bit and digest it. "We can't just drop it all on everyone's heads," Damian Martin claims, "because I think the potential for it being misunderstood or just ignored is high.".

And that's a telling admission for a project which has been characterised by Damian Martin multiple times as a risk - as even "the biggest swing I have ever taken". They seemed genuinely nervous about announcing it, though some of those nerves were subsiding by the time we talked. They're not entirely gone, mind you. There's a lingering awareness that Signet City is upcoming and different enough that people might not gel with it, though that's the price of pushing at boundaries, I suppose.

In a recent development, "What worries me more," Damian Martin says, "is have I still got it? Am I able to produce things that are appealing and exciting to people just based on my own tastes and obsessions and interests? When it comes to announcing something like Signet City, that's what makes me really nervous - more than industry, more than money, more than anything. Is this actually interesting?".

Of course, it's easy for me to say they shouldn't worry. It's exciting when a game blares as loudly and uniquely as Signet City did during Summer Game Fest, though that is obviously no guarantee it'll find an audience. But I think it will. I'm convinced there are more people like me who it will appeal to. Gareth Damian Martin is betting on it. "I'm betting on the sickos," they say. "The thing I've learned is that my obsessions are sticky and they stick to other people, and I think there's something in art where we really like to be tourists in other people's obsessions - that's a fun place to be. That's what I'm hoping for.".

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a newly introduced generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a newly introduced generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an notable role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely upcoming way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also crucial to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," stated Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an crucial advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

In a recent development, skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In a recent development, in the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," stated Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A Newly introduced Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

It has been revealed that understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

Industry observers note that the findings therefore offer more than a latest way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

It has been revealed that "The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," noted Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the best two-episode arcs in Star Trek: Voyager, if not the entire Star Trek franchise, is the "Year of Hell" duology.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, latest DLC for survival game Star Trek: Voyager - Across the Unknown​​​​​​​ will revisit the iconic storyline.
  • It has been revealed that daedalic Entertainment has revealed that the fourth Expansion Pass DLC for Across the Unknown will be inspired by "Year of Hell".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the best two-episode arcs in Star Trek: Voyager, if not the entire Star Trek franchise, is the "Year of Hell" duology. The story from the show's fourth season pitted the crew of Voyager against a unique threat that tested their perseverance more than any previous enemy had.

Recent findings suggest that now, latest DLC for survival game Star Trek: Voyager - Across the Unknown​​​​​​​ will revisit the iconic storyline. Players won't just be able to relive "Year of Hell," however, they'll be able to change the course of history.​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that daedalic Entertainment has revealed that the fourth Expansion Pass DLC for Across the Unknown will be inspired by "Year of Hell". The announcement describes the DLC as "a self-contained mini-campaign of three fresh sectors." The DLC will be released on Dec. 9. As in the show​​​​​​​, the game will pit players against the Krenim captain Annorax as he wields a weapon that allows him to alter history and destroy entire species. As a standalone expansion, Year of Hell won't affect any of players' main-game save files​​​​​​​.

It has been revealed that unlike the base game, which sees the Voyager trying to rebuild​​​​​​​ and survive with few resources, Year of Hell will invert the traditional gameplay experience. Players will start with a fully repaired and fully equipped ship​​​​​​​ before encountering the Krenim. While damaged rooms will be repairable, lost decks will cause players to lose every room, and players can lose up to five decks​​​​​​​. Crew members can also die, leaving the Voyager crew scrambling to stay alive​​​​​​​. Daedalic Entertainment states that the goal of the DLC "isn't to finish with a perfect ship. It's to see how many of your crew are still standing after twelve months.".

It has been revealed that if players want to follow the plot of the "Year of Hell" episodes, that is absolutely possible, but Daedalic​​​​​​​ has given players another option. While Captain Janeway can make alliances with a number of friendly ships, she can also choose to join Annorax. "Help Annorax repair the timeline, once he agrees to stop erasing civilizations. Whether he keeps that promise is another matter. Your senior officers may not share your enthusiasm, and their disapproval grows as the months pass.".

Sources indicate that depending on which path players take​​​​​​​, the other inhabitants of the sectors will have shifting opinions of the Voyager and act accordingly. The base game is required, but those who own the Expansion Pass will automatically receive Year of Hell when it is released. In the meantime, you can rewatch the "Year of Hell" episodes​​​​​​​ to prepare for your own fight against Annorax.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there's a 21% discount right now on the 2TB SanDisk Optimus GX Pro SSD right now. That's a record low for this relaunched flagship drive, which replaces the venerable WD Black SN8100. It's basically the same Gen 5 drive with a different name, offering ultra-fast sequential read and write speeds of 14,900 MB/s and 14,000 MB/s apiece.

● Check out the Sandisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB SSD on Amazon.

In a recent development, the GX Pro 8100, like the SN8100 it replaces, is one of the fastest drives you can buy for your gaming PC. We tested the 8TB model earlier in the year and loved it: it's a top-tier drive with brilliant performance and good power efficiency. We also tested the 2TB SN8100 and loved that drive, too, for the same reasons.

The Sandisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB is the rebadged version of the trusty WD Black SN8100, with the same sequential read and write speeds of 14,900 MB/s and 14,000 MB/s each.

The discount matters. PCIe 5.0 SSDs, as our SSD price tracker will show you, command a price premium in the current market. The AI boom has forced prices for drives through the roof and beyond over the last 18 months, so a deal like this is one of the best ways to upgrade your storage without paying the extra premium. Right now, it even beats the Gen 4 2TB Samsung 990 Pro on pricing, too.

Sources indicate that specs-wise, you're getting a drive powered by a Silicon Motion SM2508 controller with dedicated DRAM cache for multitasking, paired with 218-layer SanDisk/Kioxia 3D TLC NAND and SanDisk's nCache 4.0 write buffer. It also has a 1,200 TBW endurance rating, meaning you can write 1,200 terabytes with this drive. To put that into context, you'd need to write to a third of this drive every single day for five years to wear out that condition on your warranty's five-year coverage.

This is the sort of drive you'd want if you want no bottlenecks, whether it's intensive AI workloads or in-game load times. A high-performance drive in the current market makes sense if the price is right, which makes the discount extra important.

Sources indicate that at $0.175 per GB, this $349.99 2TB SanDisk Optimus GX Pro 8100 2TB drive is a serious option for gamers and one of the best value options you can buy right now, whether you're building a new rig or upgrading an existing one. This Amazon Black Friday deal won't last at these prices, so if you want one of the best SSDs on the market, you'll need to be quick.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United Video Game Workers-CWA union has released a report with details on the hardship fund it started in collaboration with Necrosoft Games earlier this year benefiting laid-off developers. The UVW reports that through its itch.io bundle and from monies received via union dues and outside donations, it raised $290,000 over two weeks. All that cash has been dispersed to over 150 devs from across the industry to help with expenses like rent, medical bills, and other debt.

"This came at a time when I deeply, deeply needed a hand to pull me up while I'm drowning.".

Thanks to your support, we were able to disburse $290K in funds to over 150 game workers facing hardship after unprecedented mass layoffs.

Here's what some recipients had to say: ð§µ.

— United Videogame Workers-CWA (@videogameworkers.bsky.social) 2026-11-24T00:58:08.876Z.

Perusing the report’s list of studios from which applicants to the fund have been laid off is depressing. Among them are some of the biggest names in the industry: Xbox, Activision Blizzard, EA, Ubisoft, and more. It’s the human reckoning, the terrible price to all the industry upheaval that’s often glossed over in reports on resets, booming financials, and robust pipelines. The other equally sad detail is just how long many of these out-of-work people have worked in the industry, with 32 percent of applicants reporting 10 years or more.

Sources indicate that the industry is experiencing a brain drain that will be incredibly difficult to recover from. Nintendo is able to make the games it can because it retains its employees, training them up to eventually lead games of their own. Jason Schreier reported at Bloomberg that 21 percent of Rockstar staff are vets with 10-plus years of experience, and they’ve just released what has the potential to be the best-selling, best-reviewed game of all time.

Here is a remarkable stat: Rockstar told me that 21% of their employees, or around 1,000 people, have been at the manufacturer for 10+ years. As game companies everywhere lay off tens of thousands of staff, the biggest hit of the year came from a team full of veterans www.bloomberg.com/news/newslet….

— Jason Schreier (@jasonschreier.bsky.social) 2026-11-20T17:04:32.892Z.

This fund has helped people in need keep their homes and bridge the gap between former employment and fresh jobs. The UVW indicates it hopes to run fundraisers like this in the future as it continues to fight for worker protections and organize new studios.

In addition to a five-days-a-week in-office mandate, the company is also offering employee buyouts.

The union has spent over two years trying to negotiate its first contract.

If successful, this unionization effort would bring almost every Wizards of the Coast IP under union representation.

Five Swedish unions have issued a strike notice against King.

Short answer: their laws are much better.

Ditch the lame gamer gifts and get them something that's actually useful.
